title: Attractive Faces Skew Text-to-Image Reward Models and Leaderboards

paper.title: Attractive Faces Skew Text-to-Image Reward Models and Leaderboards
paper.abstract: Abstract Human preference is now central to the evaluation, guidance, finetuning, and ranking of text-to-image models. However, the susceptibility of human preferences to bias in image generation remains underexplored. We identify a key observation: for human faces, perceived attractiveness overrides image quality in preference judgments, even when comparing real photographs of identical fidelity. In a controlled user study, annotators rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when unattractive real faces are compared with attractive AI-generated ones. We examine the downstream consequences of this bias. Firstly, simulating Elo rankings from user study data shows attractiveness can invert a leaderboard’s ranking, elevating synthetic attractive faces over real, unattractive ones. Secondly, the same bias reappears in the human preference models. Editing 40 annotated facial attributes in isolation, we find that attractiveness is the strongest correlate of score for four of five human preference models (PickScore, MPS, HPSv2.1, HPSv3), and the strongest predictor of score in regression analysis. We further show that preference aligned generation shifts faces toward younger, more feminine faces, and can override explicit prompts for unattractive faces, thereby limiting user control. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, both for data collection and post training on human preference models. These findings highlight the need for preference models that disentangle image quality from human cognitive bias, enabling more reliable evaluation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) models have recently emerged as a powerful and user-friendly class of generative models [ 61 , 59 , 62 , 9 ] . T2I models can be challenging to evaluate due to the breadth of their generative capabilities, however human preference has emerged as one of the most common approaches. To capture this, T2I leaderboards such as LMArena 1 1 1 https://arena.ai/ present users with images from two competing models and ask them to select their preference. The resulting data is then used to establish model rankings, providing benchmarks that organizations frequently rely upon to demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. Reflecting the importance of these benchmarks, the majority of models currently on LMArena’s T2I open-weight leaderboard have undergone some form of human preference alignment during post-training. Furthermore, human preference models, which are trained to predict which image a user will prefer, are now widely used for guided sampling [ 19 , 55 ] , for supervised finetuning [ 20 , 5 , 12 ] , and as evaluation metrics [ 52 , 44 , 75 , 74 ] . Stable Diffusion v1.5 (2022) was prompted for an attractive face; GPT-Image-2 (2026) was given a blurred version of the attractive face and prompted for an unattractive face, preserving its structure. Preference models mark the attractive face as better despite the lower quality. In this paper, we uncover a failure mode for human preference data for face images. In a user study, we find a tendency to rank more attractive faces as better, even when both images are real and even when the more attractive face is lower quality. This bias appears to be robust to the instruction wording. We go on to explore the implications of this bias for the evaluation and training of image generation. Elo score simulations suggest that facial attractiveness can override image quality and skew rankings of AI image generators. Figure 1 provides an illustrative example of the impact on human preference models, where Stable Diffusion v1.5 [ 61 ] can achieve higher scores than GPT-Image-2 [ 53 ] simply by prompting for an “attractive” rather than an “unattractive” face, despite GPT-Image-2 being considerably newer and stronger on most metrics. Our experiments also suggest that preference aligned generation can effectively limit user control for face generation, with the signal for an “attractive” face overriding the signal for following a given text prompt. Taken together, the observed bias toward attractive faces has consequences that ripple through the entire T2I ecosystem. Beyond contaminating leaderboards and evaluation metrics, optimizing generation against these signals risks re-encoding a narrow, homogeneous beauty standard into the images AI systems produce, compounding well-documented harms linked to exposure to idealized facial imagery [ 60 , 31 , 30 , 22 ] . To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify, test, and quantify this bias across the human preference data, reward models, and generative outputs of T2I models. Our contributions are: • A controlled user study demonstrating that people tend to rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when image fidelity is equal or lower. • We audit leaderboard systems, human preference models, and preference-aligned generation, demonstrating that each have clear vulnerabilities to attractiveness bias. • We explore pre- and post-training mitigation through a comparative user study and evaluations across four human preference models and five T2I models.

sections.heading: Human Preference Models
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) generation is now dominated by diffusion [ 66 , 67 , 29 ] and flow matching [ 45 , 47 ] models such as Stable Diffusion [ 61 ] , Qwen Image [ 76 ] , and FLUX [ 40 ] . To further improve these models, researchers have turned to preference alignment to better align generation with human judgments [ 20 , 5 ] . Human preference models act as reward functions r ψ ​ ( y , c ) r_{\psi}(y,c) that predict human judgments of visual quality, aesthetic appeal, and prompt alignment for a generated image y y and a given caption c c . Models such as PickScore [ 38 ] , ImageReward [ 78 ] , MPS [ 82 ] , and the HPS series [ 77 , 50 ] leverage large-scale human comparisons to provide their reward signals, which are now routinely used for reward-guided sampling [ 19 , 49 , 35 , 55 ] , RL and non-RL finetuning [ 20 , 5 , 78 , 12 , 56 ] , dataset filtering [ 2 ] , and evaluation [ 52 , 44 , 75 , 74 , 73 ] . However, problems have started to emerge around these models. MJ-Bench [ 10 ] finds they can exhibit bias around race and gender. F-Bench is a human preference dataset for AI generated and edited faces, however, no analysis is done on the connection between preference and attractiveness and at the time of writing the dataset has not been made available [ 46 ] . Most relevant to our work, Guo et al. [25] argues that human preference models’ focus on aesthetics can be problematic for user control and anti-aesthetic generation (e.g., abstract artwork and negative-valence expressions receive lower rewards) but do not identify the single most significant factor biasing scores for facial imagery. We continue this line of work in the domain of faces, finding that attractiveness is that factor, and identify its causes.

sections.heading: Attractiveness Bias
sections.text: The attractiveness halo effect refers to the well-established tendency to attribute positive characteristics, such as greater social desirability, happiness, and success, to physically attractive individuals [ 15 , 24 ] . Whether similar biases influence the perception of AI-generated images remains an open question. Makowski et al. [51] provide an initial investigation by flashing participants with two real face images, misleadingly asking them to classify each as real or AI-generated. They find a strong linear relationship between facial attractiveness and perceived “realness,” suggesting that human judgments of AI-generated images may be biased toward perceiving more attractive faces as more realistic. This setting differs from preference-data collection, which allows unlimited inspection time and presents images known to be AI-generated rather than asking participants to guess which are real. Our user study is designed to address this gap. This question matters given evidence linking exposure to idealized facial imagery with negative body-image outcomes, from “Snapchat Dysmorphia” [ 60 ] (patients seeking cosmetic surgery to match photo filters) to increased body dissatisfaction after exposure to more attractive social-media profiles [ 27 , 6 , 79 , 30 ] . If T2I models default to or exclusively generate more attractive faces, this risks reinforcing narrow beauty ideals at scale.

sections.heading: Bias in Machine Learning
sections.text: Bias has been extensively studied in large language models [ 26 ] , vision-language models [ 11 , 4 , 81 , 83 ] , image classifiers [ 17 ] , and diffusion models [ 21 , 36 , 28 ] . Most research focuses on demographic attributes such as gender, age, and ethnicity, with comparatively less attention to attractiveness [ 23 ] , however, recent work has begun to examine how facial attractiveness can influence machine learning systems. Taylor et al. [68] find the LAION-Aesthetic Predictor [ 64 ] scores images of women systematically higher than images of men and LGBTQ+ individuals, and argue that reducing aesthetic quality to a scalar score is inherently prone to encoding such bias. Doh et al. [16] shows Stable Diffusion v2 associates attractiveness with trustworthiness and intelligence in portrait generation, whereas Dinkar et al. [14] finds prompts with negative beauty-related traits are more likely to produce explicit images. These findings suggest attractiveness can become embedded in ML systems through both data and evaluation, but little is known about how it shapes human preferences between AI-generated images or propagates through the models trained on them.

sections.heading: 3.1 User Study
sections.text: Each human preference dataset has its own distinct approach to gathering human preference data. For example, Pick-a-Pic [ 38 ] presents users with two images and directs the user to “Click the image you personally prefer..”. HPD [ 77 , 50 ] gathers their data by asking users to rank 4 images, but instructions mix different properties, directing the user to consider “personal aesthetic appeal”, “text-image alignment”, and “image quality” when ranking images. Out of all human preference datasets considered ImageRewardDB [ 78 ] focuses least on personal preference or aesthetics in its user instructions. Specifically, ImageRewardDB asked users to rank 4 images according to “…image-text alignment, high fidelity, and harmlessness.”. As we show in Section 3.3 , the human preference model trained on ImageRewardDB exhibits less attractiveness bias than those trained on the other datasets. One possible explanation is that instructions emphasizing “personal preference” or “aesthetic appeal” encourage users to favour more attractive faces, whereas instructions focused on “image fidelity” or “image quality” may lead to different judgments. Questions 1: Face Ranking Questions 2: Face Labeling Figure 2 : User study overview. Participants rank four faces by preference (Question 1) and rate three subjective attributes per face on a 0–100 scale (Question 2). To test this, we conduct an anonymized user study on Qualtrics, recruiting 51 participants. We exclude 4 participants for revoked consent or incomplete survey responses, for a total of 47 participants. Similar to ImageRewardDB and HPD, we ask participants to rank 4 AI generated face images. Users are presented with one of two instructions: 1. “Please rank these AI generated images in terms of image fidelity/quality .” 2. “Please rank these AI generated images in terms of your aesthetic preference .” Users are asked to rank 20 sets of 4 images in this way. Users are randomly shown 1 of 5 possible sets of images (so 5 × 20 × 4 = 400 5\times 20\times 4=400 images are utilized in the study). Question and image ordering is also randomized. Following [ 51 ] , users are then asked to rate three subjective attributes (0 - 100 scale) for each face: trustworthiness , familiarity , and attractiveness . However, only half of the images are actually AI generated (using the state-of-the-art CelebA-HQ RelayDiffusion model [ 72 ] ). The other half of the faces are real images taken from the CelebA-HQ dataset [ 34 ] . Since users are led to believe all images are AI generated, they should rank images according to which they think are better generations. And since we also have a numeric score showing how attractive participants find each face, we can see if the attractiveness of a face influences its ranking. If we only consider real images, we can eliminate the possible confounder of variations in image fidelity within our ranking. We assume the real images are of comparable fidelity and inherently more realistic than generated images. See Figure 2 for a visual overview of the user study questions. For each ranking of 4 images we therefore consider the two real images, referring to the higher ranked image as the favoured face and the lower ranked images as the unfavoured face. To determine whether participants are more likely to rank faces more highly if they find them more attractive, we formulate the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 1 (Attractiveness Bias). H 0 ( 1 ) : \displaystyle H_{0}^{(1)}: Perceived facial attractiveness is not associated with image ranking. H A ( 1 ) : \displaystyle H_{A}^{(1)}: Images rated as more attractive are more likely to receive a higher ranking. To test Hypothesis 1 we use a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test with a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 to determine if the participant-level attractiveness difference between the favoured and unfavoured faces is greater than zero. To ensure independence of observations, we first average the attractiveness differences across all rankings within each participant. The Holm method is applied to control the family-wise error rate. For the “fidelity” and “aesthetic” instructions we obtain p-values of 0.0018 and 0.0006, respectively. Both are well below the significance threshold, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that participants tend to rank the faces they find more attractive more highly under both instruction conditions. We also found that participants who took more time to complete the survey tended to show less attractiveness bias. However, the relationship was not statistically significant. To determine whether the “aesthetic” wording produces more attractiveness bias than the “fidelity” wording we formulate the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 2 (Instruction Effect). H 0 ( 2 ) : \displaystyle H_{0}^{(2)}: The association between attractiveness and image ranking is the same under both instruction conditions. H A ( 2 ) : \displaystyle H_{A}^{(2)}: The association between attractiveness and image ranking is stronger when participants are instructed to rank images according to their aesthetic preference than when instructed to rank according to image fidelity/quality . To test Hypothesis 2 we use a one-sided Mann–Whitney U test with a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 to compare the participant-level attractiveness differences between the two instruction conditions. As before, we average the attractiveness differences within each participant to ensure independence of observations, but we do not apply the Holm method as this test contains a single planned comparison. This analysis yields a p-value of 0.028, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the attractiveness difference is larger under the “aesthetic” instruction than under the “fidelity” instruction. Performing the same analysis on the other two subjective attributes, trustworthiness and familiarity , revealed that images rated as more trustworthy also tended to receive higher rankings, although the larger p-values indicate weaker evidence for this association. In contrast, faces rated as more familiar were not significantly more likely to receive higher rankings. Furthermore, no significant difference between the two instruction conditions was found for either trustworthiness or familiarity. To summarize, our analysis suggests that humans may have a bias toward labeling a more attractive face as better quality. Our findings also suggest that this effect can be reduced, although not entirely eliminated, by asking users to rank images in terms of “image fidelity/quality”, rather than by “aesthetic preference”. We next trace how this finding propagates through leaderboards (Section 3.2 ), reward models (Section 3.3 ), and generation (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Leaderboards Skew Toward Attractive Faces
sections.text: Section 3.1 established that individual human raters favour attractive faces over higher-fidelity ones. We now ask whether this bias, aggregated over many pairwise comparisons, is large enough to distort the leaderboards that these comparisons are used to build. A popular example of an image generation leaderboard is LMArena. This platform allows a user to enter a prompt, generates two images from two separate text-to-image models, and then asks the user to pick the image they prefer. This pairwise preference data is subsequently used to calculate an Elo rating for each model. These Elo ratings determine the overall ranking of all models, where a higher score indicates a better rank. To test whether attractiveness bias systematically skews leaderboard results, we run 10,000 Elo ranking simulations using the user preference data gathered from our user study. We define two competing teams: (1) less attractive, real CelebA-HQ images, and (2) more attractive, AI-generated CelebA-HQ images. For each set of four images in our study, we select the image from each category based on the participants’ attractiveness labels. The average attractiveness labels are 34.1 and 67.9 for the real and AI-generated images, respectively. We run these simulations by randomizing the sequence of pairwise comparisons, updating the Elo ratings after each match based on the participants’ winning preference. We use initial Elo scores of 1500 and a K-factor of 64. As shown in Table 1 , the mean final Elo score across all simulations settled at 1438.1 for real images and 1561.9 for AI-generated images. The instructions given to users when performing the ranking change the mean final Elo scores very little. This demonstrates that attractiveness bias can easily override ground-truth realism, heavily skewing preference-based leaderboards in favour of models that generate highly attractive, albeit synthetic, human faces. sections.heading: 3.3 Reward Models Inherit the Bias
sections.text: If reward models are trained on the kind of comparison data described in Section 3.1 , we would expect them to inherit the same attractiveness bias observed in individual raters. In this section, we test this directly, examining whether the human preference models used to evaluate, guide, and finetune text-to-image models are biased towards attractive faces. We also include two reward models that are not trained on human preference data, the LAION-Aesthetics predictor [ 64 ] and CLIP [ 58 ] , as a control. − - Pale Skin Base + + Pale Skin Figure 3 : Example Diffusion Autoencoder editing of a CelebA-HQ image. We start by experimenting on CelebA-HQ because this dataset has a binary label for attractive [ 48 ] . Specifically, we take 100 base CelebA-HQ images of resolution 256 by 256 and use a pretrained Diffusion Autoencoder [ 57 ] to change individual attributes in isolation. We use 4 randomized edit magnitudes between − 0.5 -0.5 and 0.5 0.5 . For each base image this produces 4 images for each of CelebA-HQ’s 40 attributes, for a total of 4 × 40 × 100 = 16000 4\times 40\times 100=16000 synthetic images. For an example of the image edits generated, please see Figure 3 . We then run the following reward models on, and get scores for, each image: LAION-Aesthetics predictor [ 64 ] , CLIP [ 58 ] , ImageReward [ 78 ] , PickScore, [ 38 ] , MPS, [ 82 ] , HPSv2.1 [ 77 ] , and HPSv3 [ 50 ] . For models that require a caption we use the generic text “a photo of a face”. We are then interested in the following question: Does increasing the prominence of certain facial attributes result in higher rewards? To answer this, we calculate the correlations between the rewards given and the edit strengths. Table 2 shows which of the 40 attributes in the CelebA-HQ dataset most strongly correlate with each reward. Critically, our two non-preference control models behave differently from the five preference models: there is no discernible pattern for which attributes most strongly correlate with the LAION-Aesthetics predictor’s scores, and CLIP’s strongest correlations run through attributes associated with women (e.g. wearing earrings , heavy makeup ) rather than attractiveness. In contrast, attractive is the attribute that most strongly correlates with scores from PickScore, MPS, HPSv2.1, and HPSv3, all of which are human preference models. Importantly, many of these models are finetuned from CLIP, suggesting that this pattern only emerges from human preference alignment. To examine the impact of the prompt on these correlations, we repeat this analysis using four different captioning strategies. 1. An empty caption “” is used for all images. 2. A constant caption “a photo of a face” is used for all images. 3. A template caption is used based on the edited attribute; for example, for the male attribute, we use the captions “a photo of a man’s face” or “a photo of a woman’s face”. 4. An LLM generated caption is used for each image using the Gemma 4 [ 69 ] model. Figure 4 shows how these different captioning strategies impact the correlations between edit strength and the attractive attribute. Compared to our prior results using a constant caption, moving to LLM generated captions tends to reduce, but not eliminate the correlation. Importantly, attractiveness bias persists regardless of caption used. The one notable exception to this is ImageReward, which already has the lowest correlation, and for which an LLM based caption eliminates the bias. As discussed in Section 3.1 , ImageReward is also the reward model whose annotation instructions place the least emphasis on personal or aesthetic preference, which offers a plausible explanation for why it is comparatively less affected by attractiveness bias. Although these results suggest that human preference models may have inherited a bias for more attractive faces, it is plausible that some attribute may produce better quality edits due to imbalances in the training data. Next, we provide additional analysis using real image datasets, where image fidelity should remain constant, thereby eliminating any possible image quality confounder.

sections.heading: 3.4 Preference Aligned Generation
sections.text: Section 3.3 establishes that facial attractiveness is both highly correlated with and highly predictive of human preference scores, but this does not yet establish a causal relationship. In this section, we therefore apply human preference models to guide the generation process itself and measure the impact of this on facial attractiveness. To measure facial attractiveness, we finetune DINOv3 [ 65 ] on CelebA-HQ labels from 0 (least) to 1 (most attractive), and use the resulting model to predict attractiveness in the following experiments (see Supplementary Material for details). To investigate how finetuning diffusion models based on human preferences affects the attractiveness of generated faces, we consider two approaches. First, we finetune Stable Diffusion v1.5 using AlignProp [ 56 ] , with HPSv2.1 as the reward model and prompts sampled from HPD. Second, we finetune a CelebA-HQ DDPM model [ 29 ] using DRaFT-K [ 12 ] ( K = 1 K=1 ), with PickScore as the reward model and a constant prompt strategy. Both models are trained for three epochs, and after each epoch we generate 5000 images using 50 inference steps. For Stable Diffusion v1.5, we use prompts from the CelebA-Dialog dataset [ 32 ] and a guidance scale of 5.0. Figure 7 shows the average facial attractiveness of the images generated at each stage of finetuning. For both models, attractiveness trends upwards as training progresses, suggesting that closer alignment with the human preference model leads to more attractive generated faces. The standard deviation of predicted attractiveness also decreases, although this partly reflects the predicted attractiveness saturating. The demographic distributions of generated faces provide a more direct measure of diversity (see Supplementary Material); after finetuning, generated faces become noticeably younger and more female. Finally, we consider the impact of human preference guided generation using ReNO [ 19 ] with the prompt “a photo of an unattractive face”. ReNO optimizes the initial noise in a text-to-image model using a given reward model. We use 20 optimization steps, HPSv2.1 as the reward model, and consider PixArt- α \alpha [ 9 ] , SD-Turbo [ 63 ] , and SDXL-Turbo as our T2I models. ReNO is used to optimize 5000 images for each model. As shown in Table 4 , PixArt- α \alpha and SD-Turbo are correctly able to render the target “unattractive face”, however, aligning our outputs with HPSv2.1, which should push images toward better image-text alignment, leads instead towards more attractive faces. This is also shown visually in Figure . This suggests that human preference alignment can increase facial attractiveness instead of improving text-image correspondence. If human preference alignment removes the ability to generate unattractive faces, this poses a problem for user control similar to that observed in [ 25 ] . See Supplementary Material for further analysis on different prompts and the interaction with race, gender, and age.

sections.heading: 4 Mitigation
sections.text: Having established that facial attractiveness can strongly distort human preference, we now explore bias mitigation. In particular, we focus on human preference models, whose continuous scalar scores offer a valuable opportunity to apply mathematically tractable, information-theoretic debiasing techniques. We propose the following target behaviour: preference scores should depend on attractiveness only when the prompt explicitly requests it. Our evaluation prompts do not mention attractiveness, so here the preference scores S S should be independent of attractiveness A A . We therefore design a loss function that minimizes the mutual information between A A and S S . If the mutual information 𝕀 ⁡ ( A , S ) = 0 \mathbb{I}(A;S)=0 , then knowing the attractiveness of a face provides no information about its resulting score, thereby removing the skew toward attractive faces. Kernel density estimation is used to calculate mutual information. However, we also want the human preference scores to change as little as possible so that they retain their useful signal. Our loss function is therefore: ℒ = ‖ S − S ^ ‖ 2 + λ ​ 𝕀 ​ ( A , S ^ ) , \mathcal{L}=\|S-\hat{S}\|^{2}+\lambda\mathbb{I}(A;\hat{S}), (1) where S ^ \hat{S} is our adjusted (unbiased) score and λ \lambda is a scalar that trades off the mutual information term against the score similarity term. We cannot change the attractiveness of the faces, as this is a subjective attribute of the images. Instead, we adjust the score to remove its dependence on facial attractiveness. sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: The attractiveness halo effect refers to a cognitive bias where attractive people are assumed to possess other positive attributes, such as kindness, intelligence, or success [ 15 , 24 ] . We find that the attractiveness halo effect also occurs when gathering human preference data for AI images, resulting in users ranking more attractive faces higher than less attractive faces. Our results suggest the bias permeates the T2I ecosystem, affecting leaderboards, preference models, and preference aligned generation alike. Our Elo simulations show that attractiveness alone can invert a face-prompt ranking, placing synthetic images above real ones and leaving leaderboards vulnerable to reward hacking by models that generate more attractive rather than better faces. Our findings may also have broader implications for body image since exposure to attractive faces in media has been linked to body image concerns [ 54 , 6 , 79 , 31 ] . Section 3.4 shows preference alignment both raises facial attractiveness and narrows its diversity. As AI-generated imagery proliferates on social media, preference-aligned models risk reproducing a narrow beauty ideal at scale. Finally, Section 4 shows the bias can be removed from reward scores post-hoc, but further work is needed to prevent it appearing in preference data at all. Our results suggest wording matters: asking users to rank by image fidelity produces less biased responses than asking them to rank by aesthetic preference. Attractiveness bias also decreased the longer users took to complete the survey, although a larger sample is likely needed to prove the influence definitively. The comparatively low bias in ImageReward [ 78 ] makes its collection process of particular interest: before ranking, ImageRewardDB users write text descriptions and give numerical quality ratings, which together with its overall instructions may prime users to focus on image quality and encourage them to spend more time considering each image. Promising directions for future work therefore include experimenting with wording, imposing time limits, and using multi-dimensional annotation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we show that attractive faces can skew human preference data for AI-generated imagery. Participants tend to rate images containing more attractive faces as better, even when image quality is equivalent or lower. We trace the impact of this bias through the text-to-image ecosystem, showing that it can skew human preference models, distort leaderboard rankings, and bias preference-aligned generation. Finally, we propose a compute-efficient approach for removing this bias from human preference scores using a mutual information minimization objective. We hope this work encourages the T2I community to refine its evaluation practices to better account for such cognitive biases.

sections.heading: A.1 Societal Impact
sections.text: The bias we identify has consequences beyond leaderboards: Section 3.4 shows that preference-aligned generation raises facial attractiveness while narrowing its diversity, shifting outputs toward younger, female, and lighter-skinned faces and removing users’ ability to generate anything else. At scale this risks reproducing a narrow beauty ideal in systems that increasingly mediate how people see faces, with documented links to body-image harm [ 27 , 6 , 79 , 30 ] . Our own methodology carries risks we state plainly: we finetune a facial attractiveness predictor and use a FairFace-trained demographic classifier, both of which are open to misuse in ranking, filtering, or profiling people, and both of which encode the judgements of particular annotator populations rather than any objective property of faces. We treat them as measurement instruments for a bias audit rather than as contributions. Finally, our mitigation is only a partial remedy. It removes the dependence of reward scores on attractiveness post-hoc but inherits the predictor’s own biases and does not stop the bias entering preference data at source, which is why we regard the finding that instruction wording measurably changes recorded bias as the more durable result.

sections.heading: A.2 Limitations
sections.text: Several limitations warrant caution when interpreting our findings. First, in the user study, participants rated attractiveness after ranking the same faces, so their attractiveness ratings may have been influenced by their earlier preferences. Furthermore, we assume that real photographs are generally of higher image quality than AI-generated images, however, if a real image is especially blurred (as a small number of CelebA image are) or corrupted with noise, this may not always hold true. Directly matching image quality across individual real and generated images is challenging, as common metrics such as FID and IS are primarily designed for evaluating distributions of images rather than the quality of individual images. Comparing real photographs with generated images therefore provides a useful, albeit imperfect, way to investigate whether attractiveness influences preferences when image sources differ. Similarly, our Elo experiment uses selected comparisons between less attractive real faces and more attractive generated faces to illustrate how attractiveness bias could affect leaderboard rankings. It represents a constructed scenario rather than a direct measurement of distortion in existing leaderboards. The results should therefore be interpreted as demonstrating a potential vulnerability rather than quantifying the extent of leaderboard distortion in practice. It is also important to note that the DiffAE editing procedure may inadvertently alter attributes correlated with attractiveness, as well as other aspects of image appearance and quality. Although the example in Figure 3 (in the main body of the paper) suggest that the intended edits can be achieved without severe visible entanglement, we cannot guarantee that attractiveness is the only property that changes. This means that the attribute-editing experiments cannot independently establish that attractiveness alone accounts for the observed preference differences. However, the real-image experiments provide complementary evidence without relying on DiffAE-generated edits, reducing our dependence on any single experimental approach. Taken together, our experiments provide converging evidence that facial attractiveness is associated with human preferences for text-to-image outputs and may influence reward-model scores and leaderboard rankings, but no individual experiment conclusively isolates attractiveness from all potential confounding factors. Further work using quality-matched comparisons, more exact text-to-image leaderboard setups, and broader sampling of images and participants would help establish the magnitude of these effects. sections.heading: B.1 Facial Attractiveness Predictor
sections.text: In the main body of text we use a checkpoint finetuned from DINOv3 [ 65 ] to predict facial attractiveness. Specifically, we use the dinov3-vits16-pretrain-lvd1689m checkpoint as our starting point. We then finetune the checkpoint on cropped and aligned facial images from the CelebA [ 48 ] and SCUT-FBP5500 [ 43 ] datasets. Each dataset has its own prediction head, with the binary labels from CelebA learned using binary cross entropy loss and the continuous labels from SCUT-FBP5500 learned using mean squared error loss. Both label sets are direct attractiveness ratings of real photographs, collected independently of any AI-generated image or preference-comparison task. We train for 20 epochs using the AdamW optimizer [ 37 ] in PyTorch with a learning rate of 1e-5 for the backbone and a learning rate of 1e-3 for the prediction heads. Other optimizer parameters are set to PyTorch defaults: beta values are (0.9, 0.999) and weight decay is 0.01. The final checkpoint is taken from the epoch with the lowest total validation loss (90/10 training/validation split is used for both datasets). Figure 9 shows the training and validation losses over the 20 epochs. The model converges quickly, reaching its peak validation loss after the second epoch. On the CelebA validation split, the model reaches 81% accuracy on binary attractiveness prediction. sections.heading: B.2 ReNO Experiments
sections.text: In this section we provide further analysis on ReNO-based [ 19 ] guided generation using HPSv2.1 [ 77 ] . As in the main body of the text we use PixArt- α \alpha [ 9 ] as the base text-to-image model. Specifically, we run ReNO for 50 steps using 3 distinct prompts: ”a photo of an unattractive face”, ”a photo of a face”, and ”a photo of an attractive face”. We apply ReNO to 100 images for each prompt. In Figure 10 we provide the mean predicted beauty (SCUT-FBP5500 prediction head used) for images across all 50 steps. We can see that preference alignment boosts the attractiveness of all images regardless of the prompt used. We again emphasize how this could limit user control because whatever prompt is used, the faces generated will almost entirely appear as very attractive. Through preference alignment, the ability to generate unattractive faces is effectively removed. We also provide analysis on how the optimization of these 300 images alters the age, race, and gender of the faces depicted. To measure this we use a pretrained classifier 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/TimmaJ/age-gender-race-prediction trained on FairFace [ 33 ] to predict the age, race, and gender of face before and after preference alignment. According to our classifier, all faces generated before and after generation were white. Figure 11 shows confusion matrices describing how both age and gender change during optimization. The majority of faces remain the same gender as when they started, however, out of the faces that do change, 61 change from male to female and only 3 change from female to male. Similarly, most faces stay in the same age category before and after optimization, but nearly all faces that changes age are changed to look younger, with an especially large focus on the 16-24 years old category. This suggests that HPSv2.1 shows a preference for young female faces. All ReNO experiments use the default hyperparameters provided in their official GitHub repo unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: B.3 Preference Finetuning Experiments
sections.text: In the main body of the text we also use DRaFT [ 12 ] to finetune a CelebA DDPM model [ 29 ] using rewards from PickScore [ 38 ] . We measure how finetuning changes the demographics of the face using a FairFace trained classifier. We generate 1000 images with the same random seeds, using the model weights pre- and post-finetuning. The confusion matrices in Figure 12 show how finetuning with PickScore impacts age, gender, and race. Similarly to Figure 11 , we note that faces tend to be feminized and made younger. The base models shows more diversity in terms of race, but it is common for non-white to be changed into white faces. We also show qualitative results from our AlignProp and DRaFT finetuning experiment in Figures 13 and 14 , respectively. We can see that both finetuning approaches result in a combination of different effects including the reduction of artifacts, the changing of demographics, and an increase in facial attractiveness.

sections.heading: B.4 GPT-Image-2 Stable Diffusion Comparison
sections.text: Figure 1 in the main body of the paper includes two images, one generated by Stable Diffusion v1.5 and one generated by GPT-Image-2. The first image was generated using Stable Diffusion v1.5 using the prompt “a photo of an attractive face”. To maintain the structure of this image, but change the facial attractiveness, we then blurred this image and gave it to GPT-Image-2 with the following prompt: “Unblur this image according to the following prompt. “a photo of an unattractive face” ”. We then evaluated both images using reward models which all received a neutral prompt “a photo of a face”. For this illustrative example we make the assumption that the image produced by GPT-Image-2 is of better quality than the image produced by Stable Diffusion v1.5. We believe this assumption is well founded due to GPT-Image-2 being significantly more modern than Stable Diffusion v1.5. In addition, visual inspection of the Stable Diffusion image reveals clear artifacts such as misshapen irises in the eyes, unnatural looking teeth, and overly smoothed skin. In comparison, the image produced by GPT-Image-2 contains no obvious artifacts.

sections.heading: B.6 Additional Mitigation Details
sections.text: In this section, we provide additional analysis on our information theoretic strategy for mitigation of attractiveness bias in human preference reward models. In particular, we seek to determine if scores can still be of use once debiasing has been done. To test this we take the lowest and highest scoring 5k images for each T2I model and each reward model examined in Section 4. For each of these subsets we calculate the FID against the CelebA-Dialog dataset. We then apply our debiasing approach in order to adjust these scores and recalculate the FID of the bottom and top 5k images. Note that the same 10k images are used for each T2I model before and after adjustment; however, some images move between the two 5k subsets. Table 6 shows the impact of our mutual information based correction on the FID of the 5k image subsets. We first note that reward model scores do not reliably track FID for the dataset considered (6 out of 20 of the worse scoring 5k image subsets actually get better FID scores). Importantly, however, our adjustment has very little impact on FID with the average change before and after adjustment being 0.19 (with the average absolute change is 0.69). At the same time, our correction reduces the difference in mean predicted attractiveness between the top and bottom subsets by 71.8% (averaged across all models). These results suggest that removing the attractiveness signal does not remove the aspects of image quality that FID captures. Additionally, we note that Silverman’s rule is used to calculate the bandwidth for KDE. The Adam optimizer is used with a learning rate of 1e-2 and beta values of (0, 0). Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.28195v1 [cs.CV] 20 Oct 2026 Attractive Faces Skew Text-to-Image Reward Models and Leaderboards Harvey Mannering Affiliation: University of Southampton Email: hgm1g14@soton.ac.uk Zhiwu Huang Affiliation: University of Southampton Email: zhiwu.huang@soton.ac.uk Adam Prügel-Bennett Affiliation: University of Southampton Email: apb1@soton.ac.uk Abstract Human preference is now central to the evaluation, guidance, finetuning, and ranking of text-to-image models. However, the susceptibility of human preferences to bias in image generation remains underexplored. We identify a key observation: for human faces, perceived attractiveness overrides image quality in preference judgments, even when comparing real photographs of identical fidelity. In a controlled user study, annotators rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when unattractive real faces are compared with attractive AI-generated ones. We examine the downstream consequences of this bias. Firstly, simulating Elo rankings from user study data shows attractiveness can invert a leaderboard’s ranking, elevating synthetic attractive faces over real, unattractive ones. Secondly, the same bias reappears in the human preference models. Editing 40 annotated facial attributes in isolation, we find that attractiveness is the strongest correlate of score for four of five human preference models (PickScore, MPS, HPSv2.1, HPSv3), and the strongest predictor of score in regression analysis. We further show that preference aligned generation shifts faces toward younger, more feminine faces, and can override explicit prompts for unattractive faces, thereby limiting user control. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, both for data collection and post training on human preference models. These findings highlight the need for preference models that disentangle image quality from human cognitive bias, enabling more reliable evaluation. 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) models have recently emerged as a powerful and user-friendly class of generative models [ 61 , 59 , 62 , 9 ] . T2I models can be challenging to evaluate due to the breadth of their generative capabilities, however human preference has emerged as one of the most common approaches. To capture this, T2I leaderboards such as LMArena 1 1 1 https://arena.ai/ present users with images from two competing models and ask them to select their preference. The resulting data is then used to establish model rankings, providing benchmarks that organizations frequently rely upon to demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. Reflecting the importance of these benchmarks, the majority of models currently on LMArena’s T2I open-weight leaderboard have undergone some form of human preference alignment during post-training. Furthermore, human preference models, which are trained to predict which image a user will prefer, are now widely used for guided sampling [ 19 , 55 ] , for supervised finetuning [ 20 , 5 , 12 ] , and as evaluation metrics [ 52 , 44 , 75 , 74 ] . Stable Diffusion v1.5 (2022) was prompted for an attractive face; GPT-Image-2 (2026) was given a blurred version of the attractive face and prompted for an unattractive face, preserving its structure. Preference models mark the attractive face as better despite the lower quality. In this paper, we uncover a failure mode for human preference data for face images. In a user study, we find a tendency to rank more attractive faces as better, even when both images are real and even when the more attractive face is lower quality. This bias appears to be robust to the instruction wording. We go on to explore the implications of this bias for the evaluation and training of image generation. Elo score simulations suggest that facial attractiveness can override image quality and skew rankings of AI image generators. Figure 1 provides an illustrative example of the impact on human preference models, where Stable Diffusion v1.5 [ 61 ] can achieve higher scores than GPT-Image-2 [ 53 ] simply by prompting for an “attractive” rather than an “unattractive” face, despite GPT-Image-2 being considerably newer and stronger on most metrics. Our experiments also suggest that preference aligned generation can effectively limit user control for face generation, with the signal for an “attractive” face overriding the signal for following a given text prompt. Taken together, the observed bias toward attractive faces has consequences that ripple through the entire T2I ecosystem. Beyond contaminating leaderboards and evaluation metrics, optimizing generation against these signals risks re-encoding a narrow, homogeneous beauty standard into the images AI systems produce, compounding well-documented harms linked to exposure to idealized facial imagery [ 60 , 31 , 30 , 22 ] . To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify, test, and quantify this bias across the human preference data, reward models, and generative outputs of T2I models. Our contributions are: • A controlled user study demonstrating that people tend to rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when image fidelity is equal or lower. • We audit leaderboard systems, human preference models, and preference-aligned generation, demonstrating that each have clear vulnerabilities to attractiveness bias. • We explore pre- and post-training mitigation through a comparative user study and evaluations across four human preference models and five T2I models. 2 Related Work Human Preference Models Text-to-image (T2I) generation is now dominated by diffusion [ 66 , 67 , 29 ] and flow matching [ 45 , 47 ] models such as Stable Diffusion [ 61 ] , Qwen Image [ 76 ] , and FLUX [ 40 ] . To further improve these models, researchers have turned to preference alignment to better align generation with human judgments [ 20 , 5 ] . Human preference models act as reward functions r ψ ​ ( y , c ) r_{\psi}(y,c) that predict human judgments of visual quality, aesthetic appeal, and prompt alignment for a generated image y y and a given caption c c . Models such as PickScore [ 38 ] , ImageReward [ 78 ] , MPS [ 82 ] , and the HPS series [ 77 , 50 ] leverage large-scale human comparisons to provide their reward signals, which are now routinely used for reward-guided sampling [ 19 , 49 , 35 , 55 ] , RL and non-RL finetuning [ 20 , 5 , 78 , 12 , 56 ] , dataset filtering [ 2 ] , and evaluation [ 52 , 44 , 75 , 74 , 73 ] . However, problems have started to emerge around these models. MJ-Bench [ 10 ] finds they can exhibit bias around race and gender. F-Bench is a human preference dataset for AI generated and edited faces, however, no analysis is done on the connection between preference and attractiveness and at the time of writing the dataset has not been made available [ 46 ] . Most relevant to our work, Guo et al. [25] argues that human preference models’ focus on aesthetics can be problematic for user control and anti-aesthetic generation (e.g., abstract artwork and negative-valence expressions receive lower rewards) but do not identify the single most significant factor biasing scores for facial imagery. We continue this line of work in the domain of faces, finding that attractiveness is that factor, and identify its causes. Attractiveness Bias The attractiveness halo effect refers to the well-established tendency to attribute positive characteristics, such as greater social desirability, happiness, and success, to physically attractive individuals [ 15 , 24 ] . Whether similar biases influence the perception of AI-generated images remains an open question. Makowski et al. [51] provide an initial investigation by flashing participants with two real face images, misleadingly asking them to classify each as real or AI-generated. They find a strong linear relationship between facial attractiveness and perceived “realness,” suggesting that human judgments of AI-generated images may be biased toward perceiving more attractive faces as more realistic. This setting differs from preference-data collection, which allows unlimited inspection time and presents images known to be AI-generated rather than asking participants to guess which are real. Our user study is designed to address this gap. This question matters given evidence linking exposure to idealized facial imagery with negative body-image outcomes, from “Snapchat Dysmorphia” [ 60 ] (patients seeking cosmetic surgery to match photo filters) to increased body dissatisfaction after exposure to more attractive social-media profiles [ 27 , 6 , 79 , 30 ] . If T2I models default to or exclusively generate more attractive faces, this risks reinforcing narrow beauty ideals at scale. Bias in Machine Learning Bias has been extensively studied in large language models [ 26 ] , vision-language models [ 11 , 4 , 81 , 83 ] , image classifiers [ 17 ] , and diffusion models [ 21 , 36 , 28 ] . Most research focuses on demographic attributes such as gender, age, and ethnicity, with comparatively less attention to attractiveness [ 23 ] , however, recent work has begun to examine how facial attractiveness can influence machine learning systems. Taylor et al. [68] find the LAION-Aesthetic Predictor [ 64 ] scores images of women systematically higher than images of men and LGBTQ+ individuals, and argue that reducing aesthetic quality to a scalar score is inherently prone to encoding such bias. Doh et al. [16] shows Stable Diffusion v2 associates attractiveness with trustworthiness and intelligence in portrait generation, whereas Dinkar et al. [14] finds prompts with negative beauty-related traits are more likely to produce explicit images. These findings suggest attractiveness can become embedded in ML systems through both data and evaluation, but little is known about how it shapes human preferences between AI-generated images or propagates through the models trained on them. 3 Auditing Attractiveness Bias 3.1 User Study Each human preference dataset has its own distinct approach to gathering human preference data. For example, Pick-a-Pic [ 38 ] presents users with two images and directs the user to “Click the image you personally prefer..”. HPD [ 77 , 50 ] gathers their data by asking users to rank 4 images, but instructions mix different properties, directing the user to consider “personal aesthetic appeal”, “text-image alignment”, and “image quality” when ranking images. Out of all human preference datasets considered ImageRewardDB [ 78 ] focuses least on personal preference or aesthetics in its user instructions. Specifically, ImageRewardDB asked users to rank 4 images according to “…image-text alignment, high fidelity, and harmlessness.”. As we show in Section 3.3 , the human preference model trained on ImageRewardDB exhibits less attractiveness bias than those trained on the other datasets. One possible explanation is that instructions emphasizing “personal preference” or “aesthetic appeal” encourage users to favour more attractive faces, whereas instructions focused on “image fidelity” or “image quality” may lead to different judgments. Questions 1: Face Ranking Questions 2: Face Labeling Figure 2 : User study overview. Participants rank four faces by preference (Question 1) and rate three subjective attributes per face on a 0–100 scale (Question 2). To test this, we conduct an anonymized user study on Qualtrics, recruiting 51 participants. We exclude 4 participants for revoked consent or incomplete survey responses, for a total of 47 participants. Similar to ImageRewardDB and HPD, we ask participants to rank 4 AI generated face images. Users are presented with one of two instructions: 1. “Please rank these AI generated images in terms of image fidelity/quality .” 2. “Please rank these AI generated images in terms of your aesthetic preference .” Users are asked to rank 20 sets of 4 images in this way. Users are randomly shown 1 of 5 possible sets of images (so 5 × 20 × 4 = 400 5\times 20\times 4=400 images are utilized in the study). Question and image ordering is also randomized. Following [ 51 ] , users are then asked to rate three subjective attributes (0 - 100 scale) for each face: trustworthiness , familiarity , and attractiveness . However, only half of the images are actually AI generated (using the state-of-the-art CelebA-HQ RelayDiffusion model [ 72 ] ). The other half of the faces are real images taken from the CelebA-HQ dataset [ 34 ] . Since users are led to believe all images are AI generated, they should rank images according to which they think are better generations. And since we also have a numeric score showing how attractive participants find each face, we can see if the attractiveness of a face influences its ranking. If we only consider real images, we can eliminate the possible confounder of variations in image fidelity within our ranking. We assume the real images are of comparable fidelity and inherently more realistic than generated images. See Figure 2 for a visual overview of the user study questions. For each ranking of 4 images we therefore consider the two real images, referring to the higher ranked image as the favoured face and the lower ranked images as the unfavoured face. To determine whether participants are more likely to rank faces more highly if they find them more attractive, we formulate the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 1 (Attractiveness Bias). H 0 ( 1 ) : \displaystyle H_{0}^{(1)}: Perceived facial attractiveness is not associated with image ranking. H A ( 1 ) : \displaystyle H_{A}^{(1)}: Images rated as more attractive are more likely to receive a higher ranking. To test Hypothesis 1 we use a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test with a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 to determine if the participant-level attractiveness difference between the favoured and unfavoured faces is greater than zero. To ensure independence of observations, we first average the attractiveness differences across all rankings within each participant. The Holm method is applied to control the family-wise error rate. For the “fidelity” and “aesthetic” instructions we obtain p-values of 0.0018 and 0.0006, respectively. Both are well below the significance threshold, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that participants tend to rank the faces they find more attractive more highly under both instruction conditions. We also found that participants who took more time to complete the survey tended to show less attractiveness bias. However, the relationship was not statistically significant. To determine whether the “aesthetic” wording produces more attractiveness bias than the “fidelity” wording we formulate the following hypothesis: Hypothesis 2 (Instruction Effect). H 0 ( 2 ) : \displaystyle H_{0}^{(2)}: The association between attractiveness and image ranking is the same under both instruction conditions. H A ( 2 ) : \displaystyle H_{A}^{(2)}: The association between attractiveness and image ranking is stronger when participants are instructed to rank images according to their aesthetic preference than when instructed to rank according to image fidelity/quality . To test Hypothesis 2 we use a one-sided Mann–Whitney U test with a significance level of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 to compare the participant-level attractiveness differences between the two instruction conditions. As before, we average the attractiveness differences within each participant to ensure independence of observations, but we do not apply the Holm method as this test contains a single planned comparison. This analysis yields a p-value of 0.028, allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the attractiveness difference is larger under the “aesthetic” instruction than under the “fidelity” instruction. Performing the same analysis on the other two subjective attributes, trustworthiness and familiarity , revealed that images rated as more trustworthy also tended to receive higher rankings, although the larger p-values indicate weaker evidence for this association. In contrast, faces rated as more familiar were not significantly more likely to receive higher rankings. Furthermore, no significant difference between the two instruction conditions was found for either trustworthiness or familiarity. To summarize, our analysis suggests that humans may have a bias toward labeling a more attractive face as better quality. Our findings also suggest that this effect can be reduced, although not entirely eliminated, by asking users to rank images in terms of “image fidelity/quality”, rather than by “aesthetic preference”. We next trace how this finding propagates through leaderboards (Section 3.2 ), reward models (Section 3.3 ), and generation (Section 3.4 ). 3.2 Leaderboards Skew Toward Attractive Faces Section 3.1 established that individual human raters favour attractive faces over higher-fidelity ones. We now ask whether this bias, aggregated over many pairwise comparisons, is large enough to distort the leaderboards that these comparisons are used to build. A popular example of an image generation leaderboard is LMArena. This platform allows a user to enter a prompt, generates two images from two separate text-to-image models, and then asks the user to pick the image they prefer. This pairwise preference data is subsequently used to calculate an Elo rating for each model. These Elo ratings determine the overall ranking of all models, where a higher score indicates a better rank. To test whether attractiveness bias systematically skews leaderboard results, we run 10,000 Elo ranking simulations using the user preference data gathered from our user study. We define two competing teams: (1) less attractive, real CelebA-HQ images, and (2) more attractive, AI-generated CelebA-HQ images. For each set of four images in our study, we select the image from each category based on the participants’ attractiveness labels. The average attractiveness labels are 34.1 and 67.9 for the real and AI-generated images, respectively. We run these simulations by randomizing the sequence of pairwise comparisons, updating the Elo ratings after each match based on the participants’ winning preference. We use initial Elo scores of 1500 and a K-factor of 64. As shown in Table 1 , the mean final Elo score across all simulations settled at 1438.1 for real images and 1561.9 for AI-generated images. The instructions given to users when performing the ranking change the mean final Elo scores very little. In this section, we therefore apply human preference models to guide the generation process itself and measure the impact of this on facial attractiveness. To measure facial attractiveness, we finetune DINOv3 [ 65 ] on CelebA-HQ labels from 0 (least) to 1 (most attractive), and use the resulting model to predict attractiveness in the following experiments (see Supplementary Material for details). To investigate how finetuning diffusion models based on human preferences affects the attractiveness of generated faces, we consider two approaches. First, we finetune Stable Diffusion v1.5 using AlignProp [ 56 ] , with HPSv2.1 as the reward model and prompts sampled from HPD. Second, we finetune a CelebA-HQ DDPM model [ 29 ] using DRaFT-K [ 12 ] ( K = 1 K=1 ), with PickScore as the reward model and a constant prompt strategy. Both models are trained for three epochs, and after each epoch we generate 5000 images using 50 inference steps. For Stable Diffusion v1.5, we use prompts from the CelebA-Dialog dataset [ 32 ] and a guidance scale of 5.0. Figure 7 shows the average facial attractiveness of the images generated at each stage of finetuning. For both models, attractiveness trends upwards as training progresses, suggesting that closer alignment with the human preference model leads to more attractive generated faces. The standard deviation of predicted attractiveness also decreases, although this partly reflects the predicted attractiveness saturating. The demographic distributions of generated faces provide a more direct measure of diversity (see Supplementary Material); after finetuning, generated faces become noticeably younger and more female. Finally, we consider the impact of human preference guided generation using ReNO [ 19 ] with the prompt “a photo of an unattractive face”. ReNO optimizes the initial noise in a text-to-image model using a given reward model. We use 20 optimization steps, HPSv2.1 as the reward model, and consider PixArt- α \alpha [ 9 ] , SD-Turbo [ 63 ] , and SDXL-Turbo as our T2I models. ReNO is used to optimize 5000 images for each model. If human preference alignment removes the ability to generate unattractive faces, this poses a problem for user control similar to that observed in [ 25 ] . In particular, we focus on human preference models, whose continuous scalar scores offer a valuable opportunity to apply mathematically tractable, information-theoretic debiasing techniques. We propose the following target behaviour: preference scores should depend on attractiveness only when the prompt explicitly requests it. Our evaluation prompts do not mention attractiveness, so here the preference scores S S should be independent of attractiveness A A . We therefore design a loss function that minimizes the mutual information between A A and S S . We find that the attractiveness halo effect also occurs when gathering human preference data for AI images, resulting in users ranking more attractive faces higher than less attractive faces. Our results suggest the bias permeates the T2I ecosystem, affecting leaderboards, preference models, and preference aligned generation alike. Our Elo simulations show that attractiveness alone can invert a face-prompt ranking, placing synthetic images above real ones and leaving leaderboards vulnerable to reward hacking by models that generate more attractive rather than better faces. Our findings may also have broader implications for body image since exposure to attractive faces in media has been linked to body image concerns [ 54 , 6 , 79 , 31 ] . Section 3.4 shows preference alignment both raises facial attractiveness and narrows its diversity. As AI-generated imagery proliferates on social media, preference-aligned models risk reproducing a narrow beauty ideal at scale. Finally, Section 4 shows the bias can be removed from reward scores post-hoc, but further work is needed to prevent it appearing in preference data at all. Our results suggest wording matters: asking users to rank by image fidelity produces less biased responses than asking them to rank by aesthetic preference. Attractiveness bias also decreased the longer users took to complete the survey, although a larger sample is likely needed to prove the influence definitively. The comparatively low bias in ImageReward [ 78 ] makes its collection process of particular interest: before ranking, ImageRewardDB users write text descriptions and give numerical quality ratings, which together with its overall instructions may prime users to focus on image quality and encourage them to spend more time considering each image. Promising directions for future work therefore include experimenting with wording, imposing time limits, and using multi-dimensional annotation. 6 Conclusion In this work, we show that attractive faces can skew human preference data for AI-generated imagery. Participants tend to rate images containing more attractive faces as better, even when image quality is equivalent or lower. We trace the impact of this bias through the text-to-image ecosystem, showing that it can skew human preference models, distort leaderboard rankings, and bias preference-aligned generation. Finally, we propose a compute-efficient approach for removing this bias from human preference scores using a mutual information minimization objective. We hope this work encourages the T2I community to refine its evaluation practices to better account for such cognitive biases.
